topic.title: Never say 'wedding'
topic.claim: Every family planning a wedding learns to call it a 'small family function' on the phone, because the word wedding changes the quote.
topic.moment: Your cousin calls the caterer and says 'just a get-together, around 150 people'.

turn.believed: Vendors charge more because weddings are more work.
turn.actually: Vendors charge more because families won't bargain on the most emotional day of their lives.

topic.because: People don't want to look cheap at a wedding, and vendors know it. The word itself signals a buyer who won't walk away.
topic.payoff: If saying one word adds a lakh, the lakh was never for the work.
topic.behaviour: Families hide the occasion while booking venues, decor and photographers to get normal rates.
topic.mechanism: Vendors price on how little the buyer will push back, and wedding buyers push back least.
topic.group: Young adults helping plan their own or a sibling's wedding
topic.send_to: The sibling who is booking the venue next month.
topic.why_now: Wedding season is on, and every family is calling vendors right now.

score.why: Calling a wedding a 'get-together' to dodge the quote. It's a family arrangement nobody names, and the closing line stings.

topic.villain: a wedding-pricing norm that charges more to buyers who won't walk away

Wrong: 'It is currently wedding season in India.'. What's true: On 2026-11-07 the Hindu wedding season has not started. Chaturmas, when weddings are traditionally avoided, ends on Dev Uthani Ekadashi, which is Friday 20 November 2026 (some observe it on 21 November). The first main wedding muhurats come after that, around 21 to 26 November, and run into December. 2026 has an extra month (Adhik Maas), which pushes the season later than in 2025, when it started around 1 November. Some weddings still happen in early November in regions or communities that don't follow the Chaturmas restriction, so a claim of a general season would be wrong, not just early. I found no CAIT or other trade-body report of a 2026 season starting before 20 November. The post could say instead that the season is about to begin, or starts on 20 November..

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the premises is demonstrably false. Two need caveats. Premise 1 sounds universal, but the best evidence comes from US mystery-shopper tests, and only about a quarter of quotes rose when the event was called a wedding. I found no comparable study of Indian caterers. Premise 2 leaves out some legitimate non-haggling reasons for a higher wedding quote: peak muhurat dates that turn away other bookings, a higher service standard (more staff, live counters, cake-cutting or service fees), and the risk of something going wrong at a one-time event. None of that is cost of the food. Tax doesn't explain the gap either. Under Notification 11/2017-CT(Rate), as amended by 20/2019, GST on outdoor catering depends on the venue (specified premises or not), not on what the event is called. A 150-plate order with the same menu, venue and date carries the same tax whether it's a 'family function' or a shaadi.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Some vendors charge more based on the occasion, a practice called the 'wedding tax'. The word 'wedding' tells them the buyer has a fixed date, is emotionally invested and is unlikely to switch vendors, so they can charge more than for an identical spec. Mystery-shopper tests found it in a minority of cases, not across the board: Consumer Reports saw higher wedding quotes in just over a quarter of cases, and CHOICE in Australia found it at 3 of 6 venues. Part of a real wedding premium can also come from date scarcity and extra service rather than haggling power. When the menu, headcount, date and venue truly match, though, the extra amount is buyer-based pricing, not cost.

sources.quote: vendors quoted higher prices for the wedding than for the anniversary party in more than a quarter of the cases

Reports a separate Australian CHOICE shadow-shopping study in which three of six venues charged more when told a wedding was involved, for identical event specifications.

_ledger.text:
[cover] The word you hide from vendors is [the word they charge for]
Say 'wedding' on a caterer call and watch the quote move.
 

[slide 1] The word you hide from vendors is the word they charge for.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's wedding season and you're the one making the vendor calls. Laptop open on a sheet of numbers, phone on speaker, the line crackling a little.
You use your most bored voice: "Just a small family function. Around 150 people."

[slide 3] The per-plate rate comes back almost reasonable. You grin. You've always assumed weddings cost more because they're more work: more staff, tighter timings.
Then they ask about the menu, and you say "for the shaadi day" before you can stop. For a full second, the only sound is the crackle on the speaker.

[slide 4] The revised quote lands on WhatsApp that evening, about a lakh higher.
Same paneer, same 150 plates, same chafing dishes going cold by eleven. Nothing on the menu changed. Only the word did.

[slide 5] I've sat on the selling side of a quote. The caterer isn't pricing the paneer. He's pricing how unlikely you are to haggle.
One word told him the cards are printed, the relatives are watching, and you won't walk away.
Some of a wedding is real work. Not a lakh of it.

[slide 6] You forward the new quote to the family group. A thumbs up arrives. Nobody asks why the number went up.
Next on the sheet is the photographer. You dial, and the call opens: "Hi, just a small get-together at home."

[end card] Open this again before you dial the first vendor on your list.
Send to the sibling who is booking the venue next month and still says 'wedding' on the phone.

[caption] What did your family call the wedding on the phone to get a normal quote: kitty party, puja, or 'just a few friends'?

[alt text] A carousel about hiding the word 'wedding' when calling vendors. The reader calls a caterer on a crackling speakerphone and describes a 'small family function' for 150 people. The rate comes back reasonable until the reader slips and says 'shaadi', and the line goes silent for a second. The revised quote arrives about a lakh higher for the same food. The post argues the caterer isn't pricing the work but how unlikely the buyer is to haggle, since the word wedding signals printed cards, watching relatives and a buyer who won't walk away. Some of a wedding is real work, but not a lakh of it. It ends with the family group sending a thumbs up without asking why, and the reader opening the photographer call with 'just a small get-together at home'.

Mystery-shopper tests found it in a minority of cases, not across the board: Consumer Reports saw higher wedding quotes in just over a quarter of cases, and CHOICE in Australia found it at 3 of 6 venues. Part of a real wedding premium can also come from date scarcity and extra service rather than haggling power. When the menu, headcount, date and venue truly match, though, the extra amount is buyer-based pricing, not cost.

sources.quote: vendors quoted higher prices for the wedding than for the anniversary party in more than a quarter of the cases

cover.headline: The word you hide from vendors is [the word they charge for]
cover.sub: Say 'wedding' on a caterer call and watch the quote move.

paragraphs: The word you hide from vendors is the word they charge for.
slides.why_swipe: How much can one word really move a quote?

paragraphs: It's wedding season and you're the one making the vendor calls. Laptop open on a sheet of numbers, phone on speaker, the line crackling a little.
You use your most bored voice: "Just a small family function. Around 150 people."
The per-plate rate comes back almost reasonable. You grin. You've always assumed weddings cost more because they're more work: more staff, tighter timings.
Then they ask about the menu, and you say "for the shaadi day" before you can stop. For a full second, the only sound is the crackle on the speaker.
slides.why_swipe: What happens to the quote now?

paragraphs: The revised quote lands on WhatsApp that evening, about a lakh higher.
Same paneer, same 150 plates, same chafing dishes going cold by eleven. **Nothing on the menu changed. Only the word did.**
slides.why_swipe: So what is that lakh actually paying for?

paragraphs: I've sat on the selling side of a quote. The caterer isn't pricing the paneer. He's pricing how unlikely you are to haggle.
One word told him the cards are printed, the relatives are watching, and you won't walk away.
**Some of a wedding is real work. Not a lakh of it.**
slides.why_swipe: So what do you do with the rest of the list?

paragraphs: You forward the new quote to the family group. A thumbs up arrives. Nobody asks why the number went up.
Next on the sheet is the photographer. You dial, and the call opens: "Hi, just a small get-together at home."

end.save: Open this again before you dial the first vendor on your list.
end.send: Send to the sibling who is booking the venue next month and still says 'wedding' on the phone.
end.promise: How money really moves around you.

draft.caption: What did your family call the wedding on the phone to get a normal quote: kitty party, puja, or 'just a few friends'?
draft.alt_text: A carousel about hiding the word 'wedding' when calling vendors. The reader calls a caterer on a crackling speakerphone and describes a 'small family function' for 150 people. The rate comes back reasonable until the reader slips and says 'shaadi', and the line goes silent for a second. The revised quote arrives about a lakh higher for the same food. The post argues the caterer isn't pricing the work but how unlikely the buyer is to haggle, since the word wedding signals printed cards, watching relatives and a buyer who won't walk away. Some of a wedding is real work, but not a lakh of it. It ends with the family group sending a thumbs up without asking why, and the reader opening the photographer call with 'just a small get-together at home'.
